concerns.text: FR-002 states the permutation test uses a *target‑permutation* (shuffling the response variable) to compare the Full Model against a Null Model. A target‑permutation destroys the signal for both models, so it cannot isolate the contribution of interaction features. This contradicts the intended purpose of testing whether interactions add predictive value.

SC-002 requires a permutation test that directly compares the Full Model (with interactions) to the Null Model (without interactions) and assesses significance (α ≤ 0.05). This conflicts with FR‑002’s description of a target‑permutation test, creating an irreconcilable requirement.

The document refers to the three user journeys both as “User Story 1/2/3” and as “US‑1, US‑2, US‑3” in acceptance scenarios and success criteria. The identifiers US‑1/2/3 are never defined, leading to unresolved cross‑references.

SC‑007 defines the empirical p‑value as the proportion of shuffled ΔRMSE ≤ observed, i.e., the lower tail of the null distribution. Elsewhere (SC‑002) the test is described as an upper‑tail comparison (ΔRMSE ≥ observed). The opposite directions are inconsistent within the spec.
References to “US‑1” in SC‑007 (and elsewhere) are undefined; the spec only contains numbered User Stories without a US‑# scheme, causing a silent scope shift and broken traceability.

FR-002 specifies a “permutation test (target‑permutation, RMSE change as statistic)” to compare the Full Model with the Null Model. Target‑permutation shuffles the response variable, destroying all predictive signal, so it cannot isolate the contribution of interaction features. As written the requirement cannot be deterministically verified because the null hypothesis is ill‑defined.

SC-002 requires significance (α ≤ 0.05) from a permutation test comparing Full vs Null models but does not state whether the p‑value is the upper‑tail (ΔRMSE ≥ observed) or lower‑tail (ΔRMSE ≤ observed). The direction is ambiguous, making the success criterion unmeasurable without further clarification.

FR-002 and SC-002 propose using a *target‑permutation* test (shuffling the response variable) to assess whether interaction features add predictive value by comparing the Full Model to the Null Model. Target‑permutation destroys the true signal and cannot distinguish the contribution of interaction terms; it tests whether any model beats noise, not whether interactions improve performance over an otherwise identical model. A valid test should compare the paired performance of the two fitted models on the same held‑out data (e.g., a permutation of the interaction columns only, or a paired bootstrap/t-test on the RMSE differences). The current specification therefore employs an inappropriate statistical validation method for the core research claim.
